content: In the context of medical education in the United States, a medical intern is a physician in training who has completed medical school, passed Step 2 of the USMLE or COMLEX-USA, and is undergoing their first year of postgraduate training, also known as PGY-1. This term is historical, as the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) now refers to all postgraduate physicians in training as residents. However, the term intern is still commonly used in practice. In other countries, medical education typically concludes with a period of practical training similar to an internship, but the structure of academic and practical training programs, as well as the terminology used, varies significantly. For example, in the United Kingdom, the equivalent of an intern is a Foundation House Officer, though the title Foundation Doctor is increasingly encouraged. In Australia, medical graduates must complete one year of work in an accredited hospital post, known as the intern year, before receiving full registration. In Sweden, the equivalent is the allmäntjänstgöring (general practice), which is a requirement for obtaining a medical license and typically lasts 18 months to 2 years, followed by specialization training. Interns in the United States have historically been subjected to a trial by fire training process, which often includes verbal and emotional abuse, sleep deprivation, overwork, and excessive scut work. This environment has been criticized for its potential to cause mental and physical harm. Additionally, there may be unethical economic motivations behind the overwork of interns and junior residents. A medical internship typically lasts one year and usually begins in late June. There are two main types of internships: transitional and specialty track. Transitional internships, also known as traditional rotating internships, involve rotations through various specialties, such as emergency medicine, family practice, internal medicine, obstetrics/gynecology, pediatrics, and surgery. These programs are often less strenuous than prelim internships, which focus on either internal medicine or surgery for 12 months. Prelim internships, however, may provide better preparation for the second year of residency. Some residency programs, such as those in anesthesiology, radiology, physical medicine and rehabilitation, and neurology, begin at the second postgraduate year (PGY-2). In these cases, the first year of training is completed as either a prelim or transitional internship. A first-year resident in a specialty residency is sometimes referred to as a specialty track intern, such as a surgical intern for a first-year resident in surgery. In popular culture, medical internships have been depicted in television dramas such as Grey's Anatomy, where many of the main characters were surgical interns during the first three seasons. Similarly, in the show Scrubs, characters like J.D. and Elliot Reid are medical interns, while Christopher Turk and The Todd are surgical interns. These portrayals often highlight the challenges and dynamics of internship training.
